asDecan.p: Your Sun is somewhere between 20 and 29 degrees of Aquarius, the last of three ten-degree slices called decans, and in the Chaldean order this one goes to the Moon. The Moon has no dignity in Aquarius. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, so it takes its tone from the sign's ruler, which gives your feelings some of Saturn's reserve and, in modern charts, a bit of Uranus's habit of stepping back without warning. To be honest it's an odd fit, the planet of moods, memory and home lodging in a sign that likes air between people. The Five of Swords, Venus's slice, falls out with people over pride. The Six is Mercury's and thinks its way out of trouble. Yours adds a private motive, and the Moon's own Major is The High Priestess, who says very little. Look at the man in the picture, tiptoeing off with his arms full. The Star covers all of Aquarius, and this card is just your ten degrees, the ones nearest Pisces.

You're usually good company at the party and gone before anyone notices you've left. At a family dinner you're funny and involved, and then around dessert you're in the kitchen doing the dishes on your own, because you needed ten minutes where nobody was reading your face. A friend asks how you are and you give them the news, the new job, the move, and they walk off realising they've no idea how you feel about any of it. A message that wants something emotional from you sits on read for a day while you work out what you actually think. You do have feelings, strong ones, and you remember them for years, which is the Moon's doing. You just like to have them in private first and bring them out once they're sorted. From across the table that can look as though you never had them at all.

People tell you things, and it goes no further. That's the part of this decan nobody mentions, probably because the people who'd know are the ones you've kept quiet for. The Moon here knows what it is to need somewhere private, so you're careful with other people's. A friend mentions the IVF, or the job interview they haven't told their boss about, or that their marriage is wobbling, and it stops with you. You don't hint at it later or bring it up at the wrong moment, and you don't make them feel watched. You also let people change their minds without holding the old version against them, which is rarer than it sounds. At work you're the one colleagues come to before they hand in their notice. In a family you're the sibling who knows everything and says nothing, and mostly you use that kindly.

The less obvious shadow is the side door. When something bothers you, you'd usually sooner arrange your way around it than say so. Your partner's parents stay too long every Christmas, so this year you've quietly picked up a shift on Boxing Day. A colleague keeps taking credit for your work, so you start sending it straight to the manager and never mention why. It works, and that's the trouble. The other person never learns there was a problem, so they never get the chance to fix it, and you get to feel you handled it like an adult. The Seven is as much about fooling yourself as fooling anyone else, and your version is a generous account of your own motives. Sometimes the account is fair. Often you were just avoiding a conversation, and you're clever enough not to notice.

When something goes badly wrong, a redundancy, a break-up, a parent in hospital, you go calm and very private, and you start handing out versions. Your mum gets the reassuring one. Your best friend gets the funny one, the HR meeting told for laughs. Your partner gets the logistics. None of it is exactly a lie, and nobody has the whole thing. A week later you're worn out, partly from what happened and partly from keeping the versions straight, and it usually shows in your sleep first. The people close to you work out eventually that they each had a piece, and that can hurt more than the news did, because it feels like being managed. What actually helps is one person getting the full, untidy account early, before you've worked out how to tell it. After that, ordinary things, meals at the usual times and an early night.

You're more sentimental than anyone would guess. The Moon keeps things, so there's probably a shoebox somewhere with ticket stubs and a card from your first serious relationship, and you'd be mortified if a partner found it. You love with a lot of loyalty and very little announcement. What trips you up is testing. Instead of saying you feel neglected, you go quiet and wait to see whether your partner notices, and if they don't, you file it away. After a year or two there's a whole case built up that they've never heard a word of, and when it finally comes out, over a forgotten phone call, it lands on them all at once. The people who suit you notice without being told, and don't sulk when you want an evening alone. Say the small hurt out loud on the day it happens, even if it sounds petty.

The Star as your Sun card is about working for something bigger than yourself, and this slice gives it a job that's done mostly out of sight. You're good wherever discretion is the skill. Research, investigative journalism, IT security, audit, employment law, HR, the person who runs the numbers before the big announcement. You see the angle other people miss and you'd honestly prefer to work it out alone. The catch is visibility. You don't tell your manager what you're doing until it's done, and in the meantime it can look like you're doing nothing. Then the finished thing arrives, it's good, and everyone's put out that they weren't told. Over a few years that can earn you a name for going off on your own, and it comes up when promotions are decided. Send a two-line update halfway through anything that matters, even when it feels too early.

At twenty this decan usually shows up as a lot of small, tidy fibs. You were at the library, you're fine, it was nothing. Mostly they're told to avoid a fuss, and there's often a quiet drift away from a friend group that nobody quite noticed you leaving. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have worked out the difference between privacy and hiding, usually because hiding cost them something they wanted, a relationship or a friendship that went cold. They still keep their own counsel. They've just learnt to say the difficult thing before they go quiet. The fifties often bring out the Pisces edge of these degrees. People soften and become the trusted one in the family, who knows where everything's buried and has decided most of it can stay there. The risk then is holding so much for other people that nobody knows much about you.

When someone asks how you are and you feel the tidy answer coming, fine, busy, all good, add one sentence that's true and hasn't been edited. 'Busy, and a bit lonely, actually.' 'Fine, though I'm still upset about what Dad said on Sunday.' Don't explain it and don't follow it with the plan. Leave it there and let them answer. Try it for a fortnight with the three or four people who ask most often, your partner, a sister, the colleague you have lunch with.
